questions.q: Why does this lesson say GPU-backed autoscaling is a bigger cost risk than typical web-service autoscaling?
options: GPU instances are priced meaningfully higher per hour than typical CPU instances
GPU instances cannot be autoscaled at all
GPU instances are always free during off-peak hours
Web services never use autoscaling
questions.explain: The core reason: GPU compute costs meaningfully more per hour, so the same autoscaling behavior translates into a bigger bill.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what cost role does a 'max instances' ceiling play?
options: It guarantees zero downtime during deploys
It eliminates the need for caching
It only affects latency, not cost
It is the single most direct control on worst-case scaling cost
questions.explain: Max instances directly caps how much a traffic spike or bug can cost, regardless of other mitigations.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of spot/preemptible instances, as described in this lesson?
options: They cost more than on-demand but never get reclaimed
They are identical in price and behavior to on-demand instances
They are 60-90% cheaper but can be reclaimed by the cloud provider with little warning
They can only run CPU workloads, never GPU workloads
questions.explain: The discount is real and large, but so is the catch: the instance can be taken away with little warning.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do spot instances fit a queue-and-worker architecture better than a synchronous request a user is actively waiting on?
options: Spot instances are not compatible with queues at all
A reclaimed worker just means the job gets retried by another worker, rather than a user seeing an error
Queue-and-worker architectures never use GPUs
Synchronous requests are always cheaper than async ones
questions.explain: A queued job tolerates losing a worker mid-task because another worker can simply retry it -- a live, waiting user cannot tolerate that the same way.

questions.q: What question does a cost alert answer that a traffic or latency alert does not, per this lesson?
options: Whether the service is returning HTTP errors
Whether the container image built successfully
Whether the service is still cheap enough to keep running this way
Whether the load balancer is routing correctly
questions.explain: The lesson's point: a service can be perfectly healthy by traffic/latency measures and still be quietly overspending, which only a budget-based alert catches.
